title: Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis
key_facts: AI is a hot topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair, including how it can be regulated and whether AI-written text can be recognised.

Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien's debut novel was widely praised and longlisted for the Prix Goncourt, then accused of being written almost entirely with AI; he denies it and his Goncourt nomination was withdrawn.
Berkeley professor Hannes Bajohr says we must 'learn to live with doubt' and may judge texts by quality alone.
Nina George, honorary president of the European Writers' Council, says it is perverse that an author must prove a text is human-made.
US author Luke Stoffel openly used AI for his memoir, which won an IBPA award in May 2026; Coral Hart says she publishes more than 200 AI-assisted novels a year.
The German Publishers and Booksellers Association appealed to Berlin and Brussels for stricter AI regulation; more than 140 publishers signed.
quote_evidence: But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI.
"We will have to learn to live with doubt," says Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.
More than 140 publishers have signed it.
why_it_matters_hint: Proof of who wrote a book has become a central problem for authors and publishers.
notes: Feature with several views; the allegation against Orelien is unproven and he denies it. Related to C14-05 (WIRED on publishers) but a different story.
